title: Relative and subordinate clauses: אֲשֶׁר and כִּי

objectives.can: Read a clause with אֲשֶׁר, find what it refers to, and choose the right sense of כִּי.

explanation.summary: Two small words hang a great deal of Hebrew sentence structure on the clauses before them. אֲשֶׁר opens a relative clause and never changes its form. כִּי opens a clause too, but its meaning depends on the context: 'because', 'that', 'when', 'but' or 'indeed'.

sections.heading: אֲשֶׁר opens a relative clause
body: A relative clause says more about a noun, the antecedent, that stands just before it: the place which she named, the man who came. Hebrew introduces it with אֲשֶׁר, 'who, which, that'. Grammarians call it a relative particle or pronoun. The one form serves every gender, number and case. אֲשֶׁר does not tell you what its antecedent is, or what part the antecedent plays inside the clause. You find that out from the clause itself.

In Genesis 22:2 the clause אֲשֶׁר אֹמַר אֵלֶיךָ, 'which I shall tell you', is attached to one of the mountains: it identifies the mountain. In Genesis 22:3 the clause אֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים, 'which God had told him', is attached to the place, הַמָּקוֹם. Here לוֹ is Abraham, not the place. A pronoun in a relative clause does not always point back to the antecedent.

sections.heading: The pronoun inside the clause
body: Where the antecedent is the subject of the relative clause or stands in a plain relation to its verb, Hebrew often says nothing more: 'the man who came'. Where the antecedent is governed by a preposition or is the object of a different construction, Hebrew often repeats it inside the clause as a pronoun or adverb. This is called a resumptive element.

In Ruth 1:7, 'the place where she was', the antecedent is הַמָּקוֹם, and the clause is אֲשֶׁר הָיְתָה שָׁמָּה, literally 'which she was there'; שָׁמָּה, 'there', picks up the place. In Genesis 1:11 the clause אֲשֶׁר זַרְעוֹ בוֹ, 'whose seed is in it', has בוֹ, 'in it', pointing back to the fruit. In Genesis 2:11, אֲשֶׁר שָׁם הַזָּהָב is 'where the gold is', with שָׁם, 'there'. English leaves these out; Hebrew often does not.

sections.heading: Other ways to form a relative clause
body: אֲשֶׁר may have no antecedent at all: Ruth says אֶל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ, 'to where you go I will go'. With a preposition prefixed it can mean 'as' or 'where': כַּאֲשֶׁר in Ruth 1:8, 'as you have done', and בַּאֲשֶׁר in Ruth 1:17, 'where you die'. The reader decides from the sentence.

A participle with the article can do the work of a relative clause. In Genesis 2:11, הַסֹּבֵב is 'the one that goes round', and in Exodus 11:5, הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל כִּסְאוֹ is 'who sits on his throne'. The article then means 'the one who'.

In the later books of the Hebrew Bible a shorter word, שֶׁ, is attached to the next word and does the same job as אֲשֶׁר. Ecclesiastes 1:3 has שֶׁיַּעֲמֹל, 'that he labours', and Jonah 1:7 has בְּשֶׁלְּמִי, 'on account of whom'. It is very common in Ecclesiastes.

sections.heading: כִּי and its senses
body: כִּי is a conjunction that opens a clause. Its meaning cannot be read off the word, and grammarians list several senses. This lesson names the commonest. Always test the sense by asking what the clause does for the one before it.

'Because, for': the clause gives a reason. In Ruth 1:6, 'she arose … for she had heard'. 'That': the clause says what someone saw, said, heard or knew. In Ruth 1:6 the second כִּי, after 'she had heard', and in Ruth 1:18 וַתֵּרֶא כִּי, 'she saw that', are of this kind. 'When, if': the clause sets a condition or a general time, usually with a yiqtol, as in Exodus 21:2 and Genesis 4:12. 'But, but rather': after a negative, the clause gives the contrast, as in Genesis 45:8, 'not you … but God', and with אִם, כִּי אִם, in Genesis 32:29. 'Indeed': a clause or a verb may be introduced emphatically, as some read Genesis 22:17, כִּי בָרֵךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ. Others take that כִּי as 'that' after the divine oath of the verse before. Both readings are old.

Two clauses in one sentence may both begin with כִּי, with two different senses. Genesis 22:12 has כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה: the first is 'for' (the reason why the angel speaks) and the second is 'that' after 'I know'.

head: Sense of כִּי
Clue
Example
rows: the clause gives a reason for what came before
follows a verb of seeing, saying, hearing or knowing
opens the clause; condition or general time, often with yiqtol
follows a negative; gives the contrast
emphasises what follows; a disputed reading in some verses

misunderstandings: אֲשֶׁר does not agree with its antecedent in gender or number. Find the antecedent from the sense, not from the form.
A pronoun or 'there' inside a relative clause is not a mistake and not a second subject. It is the clause's way of marking the antecedent's role.
כִּי is not always 'because'. Look at what comes before it. After a verb of seeing, saying or knowing it is usually 'that'.
Do not translate every כִּי the same way within a passage. A single sentence can contain two with different senses.

deeper.heading: Is אֲשֶׁר a pronoun?
body: Older grammars call אֲשֶׁר a relative pronoun. Newer ones prefer 'relative particle' or 'subordinator', because it does not have case or gender and always needs the resumptive element to show the antecedent's function. The analysed text tags it as a subordinating word with the feature of a relative. Both descriptions lead to the same reading.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And she went forth out of the place where she was, and her two daughters-in-law with her; and they went on the way to return unto the land of Judah.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הַמָּקוֹם is the antecedent and אֲשֶׁר הָיְתָה שָׁמָּה the relative clause: 'the place where she was'. The adverb שָׁמָּה, 'there', is the resumptive element that picks up the place inside the clause.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: The name of the first is Pishon; that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two ways of making a relative clause in one verse. הוּא הַסֹּבֵב, 'it is the one that goes round', uses a participle with the article. אֲשֶׁר שָׁם הַזָּהָב, 'where the gold is', is a clause with אֲשֶׁר and the adverb שָׁם, and has no verb: the gold is simply there.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Ruth said: 'Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אֶל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ has no antecedent: 'to where you go, I shall go'. The preposition אֶל is attached to the whole clause. The second half, וּבַאֲשֶׁר תָּלִינִי אָלִין, is built in the same way. Ruth's vow is a pair of such clauses.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: Then she arose with her daughters-in-law, that she might return from the field of Moab; for she had heard in the field of Moab how that the LORD had remembered His people in giving them bread.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two clauses with כִּי. The first, כִּי שָׁמְעָה, 'for she had heard', gives the reason why Naomi rose and returned. The second, כִּי פָקַד יְהוָה, comes after the verb of hearing and says what she heard: 'that the Lord had visited his people'. The same word has two different jobs.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי is 'for now I know': the first כִּי gives the reason for the angel's command. The second, כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה, comes after יָדַעְתִּי, 'I know', and is 'that': 'that you fear God'.

practice.prompt: In אֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים (words 21–24), what is the antecedent of אֲשֶׁר, and who is לוֹ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son; and he cleaved the wood for the burnt-offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The antecedent is the ass, and לוֹ is God
There is no antecedent, and לוֹ is the place
The antecedent is Isaac, and לוֹ is the place
The antecedent is הַמָּקוֹם, 'the place', and לוֹ is Abraham, to whom God had spoken
practice.explain: אֲשֶׁר follows הַמָּקוֹם and refers to it: 'the place which God had told him of'. The suffix of לוֹ is the person God spoke to, Abraham. It does not pick up the place.

practice.prompt: In אֲשֶׁר זַרְעוֹ בוֹ (words 13–15), what does the suffix of בוֹ do?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let the earth put forth grass, herb yielding seed, and fruit-tree bearing fruit after its kind, wherein is the seed thereof, upon the earth.' And it was so.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It makes the clause a question
It repeats the antecedent inside the clause: 'in it', pointing back to the fruit
It shows that the clause is in the past
It is the subject of the clause
practice.explain: The clause says that the seed is 'in it'. אֲשֶׁר by itself does not show how the fruit relates to the clause, and so Hebrew puts a pronoun in the clause.

practice.prompt: What is שֶׁיַּעֲמֹל (word 5) in this late book?

quoted.title: Ecclesiastes
quoted.english: What profit hath man of all his labour wherein he laboureth under the sun?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A relative clause: שֶׁ is a short form that does the work of אֲשֶׁר, 'which he toils'
A conjunction that begins a question
practice.explain: The שֶׁ is attached to the verb יַעֲמֹל. It is the later and shorter way of saying אֲשֶׁר, and the clause describes עֲמָלוֹ, 'his toil'.

practice.prompt: Which sense of כִּי (word 0) fits best at the head of this law?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: If thou buy a Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve; and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'when' or 'if': the clause sets up the case the law covers
practice.explain: The clause opens the law and has a yiqtol, תִקְנֶה, 'you buy'. It states the conditions under which the rule applies. A reason would follow something already said.

practice.prompt: What does כִּי (word 6) do after לֹא אַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם אֹתִי?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God; and He hath made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces the contrasting fact: 'but God'
practice.explain: After a negative statement, כִּי names what is true instead. Joseph says that his brothers did not send him: 'but God' did.

check.prompt: What sense of כִּי (word 1) does this verse need?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And when she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, she left off speaking unto her.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The clause says what she saw: that Ruth was determined to go with her. After a verb of seeing, saying or knowing, כִּי is usually 'that'.

check.prompt: What does כִּי (word 9) do in Naomi's request to be called Marah?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And she said unto them: 'Call me not Naomi, call me Marah; for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It gives the reason for her request: 'for the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me'
It means 'that', after a verb of knowing
check.explain: The clause explains why she wants to be called Marah, 'bitter'. It follows a command and gives its ground.

check.prompt: What sense of כִּי (word 0) is it here, and what follows?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a wanderer shalt thou be in the earth.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'when': whenever you till the ground, it will not yield its strength
check.explain: The clause sets a general condition with a yiqtol, תַעֲבֹד. The main clause says what will then be the case.

check.prompt: What does כִּי אִם (words 6–7) mean after לֹא יַעֲקֹב יֵאָמֵר עוֹד שִׁמְךָ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'but', or 'but rather': it names what the name will be instead
check.explain: After a negative, כִּי אִם means 'but' or 'except'. The name will no longer be Jacob; it will be Israel.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: and all the first-born in the land of Egypt shall die, from the first-born of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the first-born of the maid-servant that is behind the mill; and all the first-born of cattle.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A participle with the article, working as a relative clause: 'who sits on his throne'
check.explain: The article with a participle often means 'the one who …'. The phrase says which first-born is meant: the first-born of Pharaoh who sits on the throne.

check.prompt: What is the antecedent of אֲשֶׁר (word 22) in אֲשֶׁר אֹמַר אֵלֶיךָ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And He said: 'Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: אַחַד הֶהָרִים, one of the mountains
אֶרֶץ הַמֹּרִיָּה, the land of Moriah
check.explain: God says that he will tell Abraham which mountain. The clause identifies the mountain and stands just after it.

check.prompt: What does כַּאֲשֶׁר (word 13) mean in Naomi's blessing?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Naomi said unto her two daughters-in-law: 'Go, return each of you to her mother's house; the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The prefix כְּ, 'like', joined to אֲשֶׁר, 'which', gives 'as'. Naomi wishes the Lord to deal with them as they have dealt with her and with the dead.

check.prompt: Naomi says אַל בְּנֹתַי, 'no, my daughters' (words 10–11), and goes on with כִּי (word 12) מַר לִי. Which sense of כִּי fits?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: would ye tarry for them till they were grown? would ye shut yourselves off for them and have no husbands? nay, my daughters; for it grieveth me much for your sakes, for the hand of the LORD is gone forth against me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'because': it is bitter for her more than for them
check.explain: After אַל, 'no', my daughters, the clause gives her reason: 'for it is much more bitter for me than for you'. It is a reason and not a report of something she said.

reading.why: Eight verses with a relative clause (the place where she was), 'for' and 'that' clauses with כִּי, and the conversation of the road. The two main uses of כִּי sit side by side.
